text:
Many markets outside of the US didn't have a lot of availability for 6000 series cards, at least not at similarly good discounted pricing, so even the 7700 XT is selling surprisingly well in some places. 

That being said, I would strongly urge people to be patient and wait for the 7800 XT to become available at a price which is close to the MSRP, or a 6800 XT that's close to 500 or less. I would expect the 7800 XT to prove to be a better value than the 6800 XT in the long run, given that it has a newer architecture with some new features, and might get better quality upscaling than the older Radeon cards at some point. Even a 550 USD model of the 7800 XT is going to be a better value than a 7700 XT at 450 for most users, especially if it's actually a higher quality model of 7800 XT with a better cooler, though the value advantage over the 4070 is getting a bit closer at that point, as the 4070 definitely does still have a long list of useful features, many of which are likely to be valuable to most users. 

The 6800 at around the same price as the 7700 XT or less is almost definitely going to offer better long term value than the 7700 XT, because the larger Vram buffer is likely to matter more than the various features, though the 7000 series might eventually get better upscaling quality than the older Radeon cards. 

I think that from a marketing standpoint, the 4070 would have made more sense with 16GB of RAM. People would be a lot more willing to pay a premium for all of those various Nvidia features, and the lower power consumption, if the 4070 didn't lack that one very obvious features, the Vram capacity. The 4070 ti would also look a lot more competitive against the 7900 XT with 16GB of Vram, because I think most people would not consider the difference between 16GB and 20GB to be a big deal, whereas 12GB is a lot more likely to be a limiting factor with the 4070 ti.

text: @Altrop  You are confusing a lot stuff, "no need for fps cap" in regard to limit the power draw. I usually use gsync and RTSS framecap at the upper limit of my display's max refresh to avoid tearing. The max 150W was while running the GPU under full load with MSI Kombustor. The stress test quickly reveals stability issues in form of artifacting while dialing in the under volt. Power draw in games varies of course and isn't as sustained. I wasn't even that luck with the silicon lottery, other people manage to go as low as 900mV. The OEM's are usually very conservative for the sake of stability. They use a safe voltage curve, which is fine for most of their yield. You only change the voltage curve, while not touching the clocks. This provides the same performance as stock with less power draw. Once the undervolt is stable, one can try to raise the clocks for a little bonus. author: @Lightkie

text:
It's likely the non-monolithic die approach and perhaps the manufacturing process too. Currently Nvidia still uses monolithic dies, since it has not gotten old or anything, and they also have a great manufacturing process in use. AMD cut costs by using a different process (in nanometres) for the memory and whatelse and more modern one for the graphics cores, which is interesting from a design perspective, but when data (as in electricity) crosses the chips that are connected in the die, this likely is more costly in power than they wished it would be. RX 7600 is monolithic and just a bit more powerful than RX 6600 XT and consumes about as much, but it's made with the same 6 nm process as far as I know, which tells that it's the process, as usual, which gives the efficiency benefit, not the architecture, at least in this case.
 Naturally the numbers look bad against Nvidia, but the two cards in this video do not in my opinion consume too much power to cause problems, though fitting them in small and hot cases is not that appealing.

text:
You are right in two aspects: Yes, there is almost always room for improvement on the software side of things. And yes, the current generation of GPUs (if you exclude the very top end) is pretty lackluster in terms of value vs. its predecessors.

However, the whole story of "bah, all games unoptimized - bad!" is completely missing the point and just plain wrong. The vast majority of games is developed (and has been for a very long time) with consoles in mind. That sets a very clear and predictable hardware envelope for the developers. For consoles, on the one hand they cannot exceed that hardware, on the other hand they can very specifically test for that.

Now, historically PC components made up for the disadvantage of being much more diverse than consoles (and hence very hard to test for) by being, in general, more powerful - with that lead increasing to almost ridiculous levels of superiority as we're coming upon the end of a console cycle. That's the headroom developers used for PC gamers to have better visuals and a high refresh rate experience.

Right now, we're nowhere near these levels of superiority comparing PC vs. consoles, and probably won't even be in the next CPU/GPU gen. Both PS5 and xBox have drastically improved hardware. This makes the notion of expecting mid-range PC hardware to be capable of delivering high refresh rate gaming with improved visuals in 4K when running the same games just silly. It's not going to happen, no matter what level of optimization the software gets, because there's just not enough computational headroom left.

Besides, PCs already need to be more powerful than consoles in the first place, just to deliver the exact same experience, because they are handicapped by not being purpose-built. They lack unified memory which leads to data being shuffled around from storage to RAM to VRam (consoles don't need to do that), they have to use CPU capacity to decompress assets when streaming them in (consoles have purpose-built ASICs for that), and they have a software (and hardware!) base that is inherently diverse. In short: PCs already need to be more powerful to be on equal footing, and only once you're across that threshhold they have headroom for being better.

Don't expect the days of PC vs. PS3/360 or PC vs. late PS4/One to come back anytime soon, unless you count PC as always being "13900K/Zen4-X3D + 4090 + 32 to 64 GB ultrafast DDR5".

Percent math is quite normal so long as you are consistent with the comparison.  I actually fear the way you're doing it is the opposite and makes it more confusing.  
So, % difference = (State_2 - State_1)/State_1.  If GPU 1, the thing we're trying to compare, so in this case the 7700 XT, got 100 FPS.  If you say "10% higher" (+10%), that means 10 FPS more (110 FPS).  If you say 10% lower (-10%), it's still -10 FPS (90 FPS).  The math is actually very consistent.  Now, if you change your base comparison to now use a different denominator, that's when things get screwy.  If you now did GPU 2 (110 FPS) as your basis (which is what you've done in the charts by flipping the comparisons), the math is (100-110)/110 ~ -9%.
